Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a pl
item.content:encoded:
Jesús David Castellano / @_JDCastellano
Willson Contreras se convirtió en el líder espiritual de los Medias Rojas de Boston en lo que fue un camino transformador que pasó de una virtual catástrofe a la clasificación a postemporada por segundo año consecutivo.
Y es que tras finalizar la jornada del 17 de junio con récord de 29-42, los Medias Rojas ganaron 55 de sus siguientes 85 juegos —la mayor cantidad de todo el béisbol— para mejorar su foja a 84 victorias y 72 derrotas y sellar su boleto a playoffs el pasado domingo, luego de que los Bravos de Atlanta ayudaran venciendo a los Astros de Houston.
Los Medias Rojas no pudieron celebrar con un triunfo en el bolsillo. Cayeron ante Tampa Bay en el último de la serie en Tropicana Field, pero eso poco importó, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta todo el camino recorrido para anotar su nombre en la fiesta de octubre luego de estar destinados al desastre en los primeros tres meses de zafra. Sencillamente nunca se rindieron, y eso lo reconoce Willson y se lo hace ver a sus compañeros.
«Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido»
«Primeramente, darle las gracias a Dios por todo lo vivido este año. Un año bastante bendecido y acontecido», dijo Willson a El Extrabase durante la celebración en el clubhouse visitante del Tropicana Field. «También hay que agradecer por el equipo que tenemos alrededor, los muchachos, la clase de personas que tenemos. Y de verdad que nunca dejamos de trabajar, ni de perseguir ese cupo a los playoffs».
En un buen tramo de la campaña, el primera base carabobeño comandó a la ofensiva patirroja. Primeramente, despuntó bateando por encima de .300 en abril y luego mantuvo la constancia suficiente como para terminar encabezando al equipo —con seis compromisos por disputar en el calendario regular— en cuadrangulares (27), carreras impulsadas (81), porcentaje de embasado (.387), slugging (.518) y OPS (.905).
Su escolta en el renglón de vuelacercas fue Wilyer Abreu (24), que no solo aportó con el bate, sino con su prodigiosa defensa en los jardines que lo tiene como firme candidato a obtener su tercer guante de oro consecutivo.
Elogios para Abreu y Monasterio
«Estoy orgulloso de todos mis compañeros, especialmente de Wilyer; por todo lo que ha hecho este año y lo que ha logrado, ha sido bastante importante, igual que (Andruw) Monasterio, que lo trajeron para acá a hacer un trabajo. Se amoldó muy bien a su rol y mira, esto es lo que hace un equipo unido, clasificar», añadió.
«Estoy verdaderamente orgulloso del equipo que formamos y que tenemos ahora mismo», acotó Wilyer, que comanda a los jardineros derechos de la Liga Americana en Carreras Salvadas a la Defensiva con 26. «Le dimos la vuelta a la temporada de una forma increíble. Me siento orgulloso de haber sido parte de esto, de poder ayudar y contribuir al equipo en este momento y durante toda la temporada».
Wilyer también destaca entre los jugadores de su posición en el nuevo circuito siendo segundo en Outs Por Encima del Promedio (3) y primero en valor en carreras de fildeo (5). Igualmente, despunta en asistencias desde los jardines (12) y en el apartado ofensivo, lidera a los Medias Rojas en carreras anotadas (81), dobles (36, con lo que comanda la Liga Americana) y bases por bolas (70). El zuliano estableció topes personales en las categorías ofensivas antes mencionadas, además de traídas al plato (74), imparables (144) y, por supuesto, bambinazos (24).
Monasterio ha entendido su rol
Por su parte, Andruw Monasterio supo adaptarse a su rol de pelotero de reemplazo, con tramos destacados a la ofensiva. Un ejemplo de ello fue julio. En ese entonces asumió la titularidad de las paradas cortas en ausencia del lesionado Trevor Story, lo que coincidió con la racha de 15 triunfos seguidos que le dio vida a Boston. Exhibió un promedio de .338 (de 65-22), OBP de .413, slugging de .631 y OPS de 1.044, con tres cuadrangulares, 11 producidas y nueve anotadas.
Pero no se limitó al campo corto; Monasterio también vio acción en segunda, en primera, e incluso en tercera.
«Para mí, todo fue amoldarme a mi rol», comentó Monasterio a El Extrabase. «Fui al Spring Training y me gané el puesto. Súper contento porque son cuatro años en el show y cuatro años clasificando, es una bendición. Es muy satisfactorio, porque tú trabajas mucho para esto, para este momento del año, el béisbol en octubre».
Suárez ha sido clave en el tramo final
En el renglón del pitcheo, Ranger Suárez ha sido clave en este tramo final de la zafra, luego de presentar altibajos durante gran parte del año e incluso estar en lista de lesionados después de la pausa del juego de estrellas.
En sus últimas cinco aperturas exhibe foja de 3-1 y una efectividad de 2.70 en 30 innings de labor, con 22 ponches, 12 pasaportes y un WHIP de 1.27. Todo eso ha confluido en una actuación general en su primera contienda en la Liga Americana, en la que posee un promedio de carreras limpias de 3.27 en 143.1 capítulos de trabajo a lo largo de 27 salidas.
«Contento del sacrificio que hicimos durante la temporada, especialmente por cómo empezamos», expresó el zurdo de Pie de Cuesta. «Entonces, mira lo que nos recompensó Dios, estamos en los playoffs».
A Ranger se lo ha caracterizado por ser un lanzador bastante calmado, casi imperturbable. Y bastante de eso mostró el equipo para lograr revertir su situación de inicio de temporada. «No comenzamos de la manera que queríamos, pero el talento de los muchachos es increíble. Sabíamos que le íbamos a dar vuelta a la situación».
Sigue la cobertura por El Extrabase

item.title: [NESN] Red Sox's Willson Contreras Happy With Earlier Coaching Changes | NESN
item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan
item.description: After what once seemed like an impossible outcome, the Boston Red Sox officially clinched a playoff spot, a very exciting moment for a team that has a real chance to win it all. A few months ago, it seemed like the Red Sox didn’t have a chance to come close to accomplishing this feat, but they did exactly that because of some of the decisions ownership made. Ultimately, while those decisions were questioned, the Red Sox decision-makers clearly made the right move by parting ways with Alex Cora.
item.content:encoded:
After what once seemed like an impossible outcome, the Boston Red Sox officially clinched a playoff spot, a very exciting moment for a team that has a real chance to win it all.
A few months ago, it seemed like the Red Sox didn’t have a chance to come close to accomplishing this feat, but they did exactly that because of some of the decisions ownership made. Ultimately, while those decisions were questioned, the Red Sox decision-makers clearly made the right move by parting ways with Alex Cora.
Speaking to reporters, it sounded like players in the clubhouse felt the same way. Willson Contreras, a longtime veteran and a big part of the Red Sox playoff push in the second half, said the staff change affected the chemistry and that all they needed was time.
The Red Sox proved that to be true.
“New staff, same energy, same grinding staff,” Contreras said of the early season changes that rocked the club, per The Athletic. “We created a family here with good chemistry throughout the season. We just needed time. And the time came for us.
“The most important thing to me is that everybody never stopped working. Everyone was finding their way to make an adjustment and play their game the right way. This is what we play for. This is just the first step ahead to get to the postseason. I just wanted everyone to know that I’m proud of every one of you. It’s a long season. We played through injuries, we played through a staff change, but we never stopped believing, and that’s why we’re here.”
Right now, barring something drastic, the Red Sox will play the New York Yankees in the Bronx.
This is going to be a crazy series, as many could argue that these are the two best teams in the American League.
Whoever wins this series has to feel pretty good about making the World Series, though there’s still a lot that has to happen before making any assumptions. The Tampa Bay Rays also seem to be very good.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Who matters most for Red Sox in playoffs? We ranked the top 10
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history. But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way. It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes raz
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.

item.title: [bostonglobe.com] Red Sox offense has been running on fumes down the stretch - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have secured a spot in baseball's postseason, making history by becoming the first team to clinch a playoff berth after being 14 games below .500. As of Sunday (September 20), the Red Sox have achieved an 84-72 record under interim manager Chad Tracy, following a remarkable second-half surge. Their playoff spot was confirmed with the Houston Astros' loss to the Atlanta Braves.
Despite a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays, the Red Sox celebrated their postseason berth with a clubhouse party. The team, led by spiritual leader Willson Contreras, has shown resilience throughout the season. Tracy, who took over from Alex Cora on April 26, has been credited with stabilizing the team and fostering a supportive environment.
The Red Sox's journey to the playoffs included a significant turnaround starting with a four-game sweep of the New York Yankees in late June. They went on to achieve a 15-game winning streak, tying a franchise record set in 1946. This impressive run has positioned them as the No. 5 seed, likely facing the Yankees in the AL Wild Card round.
The team overcame early-season challenges, including the dismissal of Cora and several coaches. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow emphasized the importance of decisive action in creating a thriving environment for the players. Looking ahead, the Red Sox aim to continue their momentum into the postseason, with the first game of the Wild Card Series expected to take place at Yankee Stadium on September 29.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Shares Honest Message After Red Sox Clinch originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Willson Contreras never stopped believing in the Boston Red Sox.
After Boston clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB postseason Sunday, the veteran first baseman reflected on the team's journey and made it clear how proud he is of the clubhouse.
"I did believe in my team," Contreras said in an interview. "I did believe in everybody who was here. I never had a doubt that we can turn the season around."
Contreras recalled sending a message to his teammates during Boston's struggles.
"I just said, 'Keep believing in ourselves,'" Contreras said, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. "I said, 'Believe.' That was our main word. And that's what we believed from Day 1."
The Red Sox eventually turned their season around, but Contreras credited the entire clubhouse for continuing to work through adversity.
The full speech from Willson Contreras to the team. Electric stuff. Clearly the guy who leads this entire group. Of course he had to throw a trash barrel lol. https://t.co/pF1S0TpPyz
— Tyler Milliken (@tylermilliken_) September 20, 2026
"We created a good family here, good chemistry throughout the season," Contreras said. "We just needed time and the time came for us."
Contreras also pointed to the injuries and other challenges Boston faced throughout the season.
"We played through injuries, we played through mental stuff, physical stuff but we never stop believing in each other and that's why we're here," he said.
Contreras joined the Red Sox from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason and quickly became an important voice in the clubhouse.
Following Sunday's clinching celebration, he addressed his teammates and made sure they knew how much he appreciated the group.
"I'm really thankful, first of all, for playing for Boston," Contreras said. "Thankful for the front office for asking me to come here and all of the good human beings that are here on this team."
For Contreras, reaching the postseason is an accomplishment worth celebrating, but he views it as only the beginning.
"This is just the first step ahead," Contreras said. "I just wanted to let everybody know that I'm proud of every one of you."

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell
item.description: The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series. "Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not
item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox avanza a playoffs
Roman Anthony: "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos"
Boston es el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial, desde 1903
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida.- . "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos", dijo Roman Anthony en medio de la celebración de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por su pase a la postemporada.
Mientras los Boston Red Sox celebraban su improbable clasificación a la postemporada en el Tropicana Field, con champán y cerveza a raudales, la música del vestuario parecía la más apropiada.
"Stayin' Alive".
"Creo que eso lo dice todo", declaró el jardinero izquierdo Roman Anthony el domingo, de acuerdo a un reporte de ESPN.
El 24 de junio, los Red Sox tenían un récord de 32-46 y estaban a 15 juegos y medio del liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Desde entonces, han logrado un récord de 52-25 y se clasificarán para los playoffs.
Los Red Sox perdieron 5-1 contra los Tampa Bay Rays en el último partido de su serie, por lo que no pudieron asegurar su pase. Sin embargo, aproximadamente una hora después de que terminara el partido, los Houston Astros perdieron 4-2 contra los Atlanta Braves, lo que permitió a los Red Sox asegurar su lugar como comodín.
Poco después de que se confirmara el resultado del partido Astros-Braves, los jugadores, entrenadores y personal de los Red Sox se reunieron cerca del montículo del Tropicana Field para una foto de equipo.
"Realmente no me importa cómo entramos, lo importante es que entramos", dijo el campocorto Trevor Story.
Los Red Sox son el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial (desde 1903). Dos de los tres casos anteriores llegaron a la Serie Mundial, con los Boston Braves ganándola en 1914.
El manager interino Chad Tracy estuvo al mando durante gran parte de la remontada de este año. Desde su nombramiento el 26 de abril tras el despido de Alex Cora, los Red Sox tienen un récord de 74-55.
"Miren, no estábamos en una buena situación", dijo Tracy. "No estábamos jugando bien. Pero esto demuestra que si uno persevera, pueden suceder cosas buenas. No podría estar más orgulloso de este grupo".
El primera base Willson Contreras dijo que mantuvo la fe, incluso cuando las cosas iban mal, y la recompensa fue dulce.
“Es difícil no emocionarse hasta las lágrimas”, dijo Contreras. “Es un gran logro, pero no quiero que este equipo se detenga aquí. Quiero seguir adelante. Hemos demostrado que se puede estar en racha y superar grandes obstáculos”.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Roman Anthony Makes Personal Admission After Playoff Clinch
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox lost to the Rays 5-1 on Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field. The game itself did not matter. What happened later did. The Braves beat the Astros to eliminate Houston from wild card contention, and the Red Sox' postseason berth became official. Players pulled on celebration gear and goggles, posed for a team photo on the field, and returned to a locker room that erupted in champagne and beer. For one player in particular, the moment carried weight that went beyond the standings
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox lost to the Rays 5-1 on Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field. The game itself did not matter. What happened later did.
The Braves beat the Astros to eliminate Houston from wild card contention, and the Red Sox' postseason berth became official. Players pulled on celebration gear and goggles, posed for a team photo on the field, and returned to a locker room that erupted in champagne and beer.
For one player in particular, the moment carried weight that went beyond the standings.
Anthony Gets His Moment
Roman Anthony was on the roster for last year's Wild Card Series against the Yankees. He never got to play in it. An injury kept him off the field for the biggest games of the season, and he could only watch as Boston's run ended in three games.
This year brought another injury. Anthony missed significant time before fighting his way back in August. When the celebration started Sunday, he was in the middle of it.
"I felt this a little bit last year but obviously being injured, I am so happy to be part of it now," Anthony said. "It's just an amazing feeling. Obviously, we wanted to win, but the way it happened, being together watching that game, it was amazing."
The emotion was real. Anthony has dealt with two straight seasons of injury setbacks during the most important stretches. Getting to celebrate with his teammates, healthy and contributing, meant something different for him than it did for most of the room.
Tolle Reflects on How Far The Red Sox Have Come
Payton Tolle was one of the last players to speak with reporters after the celebration had settled. His perspective captured what the locker room was feeling.
"I think it was just relief," Tolle said. "I think there's also just that feeling of like, 'Man, we've come a long way.' You know, we're going to enjoy this and be proud of it. It was a whole lot of fun."
"Obviously, you want to win, but being in is the most important thing," Tolle added.
The big left-hander has been one of the best stories of Boston's season.
Tracy and Contreras Address the Room
Chad Tracy took in the scene from the side of the room before addressing what his team had accomplished.
"At the beginning, we had a long way to go," Tracy said. "It's like, 'How do we get on track and get things moving in the right direction?' When the end of June hit and things started to go, and we started to see things come together, it became very much on our mind. So I'm just really happy for our guys."
"They stared almost an impossible task right in the face, and they refused to take no for an answer," Tracy said. "They're very battle tested, and I'm super, super proud of them."
Willson Contreras called for silence and delivered a message to his teammates.
"We create a good family here, good chemistry throughout the season," Contreras said. "We just needed time, and the time came for us. And what's the most important thing to me is that everybody never stopped working. Everybody was finding a way to make adjustments and play the game the right way."
"This is what we play for," Contreras said. "This is why we're here."
The room answered with a roar, and the celebration picked back up.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24. They are in the playoffs with six games to spare.
The words from Sunday's locker room told the full story. Relief from Tolle. Pride from Tracy and Contreras. Gratitude from Anthony, who finally gets to experience what he missed a year ago.
This team earned every drop of champagne. What comes next starts September 29.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Roman Anthony Makes Personal Admission After Playoff Clinch appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox All-Star Willson Contreras Has Strong Message Ahead of Playoffs
item.dc:creator: Scott Roche
item.description: When the Boston Red Sox lost two out of three games to the Colorado Rockies in late June, it felt like rock bottom in the 2026 season. However, what followed shocked many in baseball. Two lengthy winning streaks later, one that wrapped around the MLB All-Star break, the Red Sox climbed into an American League wild-card spot and never looked back. In fact, they built such a big lead for the second wild-card spot that they have survived a rough September to lock down a playoff berth. After a 5-1 l
item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox lost two out of three games to the Colorado Rockies in late June, it felt like rock bottom in the 2026 season. However, what followed shocked many in baseball.
Two lengthy winning streaks later, one that wrapped around the MLB All-Star break, the Red Sox climbed into an American League wild-card spot and never looked back. In fact, they built such a big lead for the second wild-card spot that they have survived a rough September to lock down a playoff berth.
After a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday afternoon, Boston watched from the clubhouse as the Atlanta Braves completed a sweep of the Houston Astros, which officially clinched a playoff berth for the Red Sox. As the celebration was happening in the clubhouse, first baseman Willson Contreras had a message for his teammates.
Boston Red Sox First Baseman Willson Contreras Drops Honest Quote After Clinching Playoff Berth
Nearly midway through the season, the Red Sox were 32-46, buried in last place in the AL East and the wild-card standings. Then, all of sudden, a switch went off and they made history. According to Ian Browne of MLB.com, Boston is the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 46 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it.
As far as Willson Contreras goes, the All-Star first baseman didn’t mince words about his teammates and believing in his teammates.
“I did believe in my team,” said Contreras, per Browne. “I did believe in everybody who was here. I never had a doubt that this team would get to the position we are in. At one point, I texted the team and I just said, ‘Keep believing in ourselves.’ I said, ‘Believe.’ That was our main word. And that’s what we believed from Day 1.”
Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals in a trade last winter. Some thought he might have been traded at the deadline in August. However, Boston’s winning streak around the All-Star break squashed those thoughts. He has been the leader this season for the Red Sox as the season has gone along.
Contreras missed the Rays series over the weekend. He was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas Rangers last week. He remains day-to-day as the postseason inches closer.
Boston Red Sox on Collision Course Against New York Yankees
All signs point to an AL wild-card series between Boston and the New York Yankees. Tampa Bay’s magic number to clinch the AL East is two. They have a four-game series against the Yankees in the Bronx, and one win officially clinches it.
It would be the second straight season the two rivals would meet in the wild-card round in New York. Boston has two series remaining at home before the playoffs. They will host the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs in a pair of three-game series. Interim manager Chad Tracy will likely use that time for rest and lining up his rotation for the postseason. That didn’t seem possible just three months ago.

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — As the Boston Red Sox celebrated an improbable postseason berth at Tropicana Field, with Champagne and beer flowing all around, the clubhouse soundtrack seemed appropriate.
“Stayin’ Alive.’’
“I think that pretty much says it all,’’ left fielder Roman Anthony said Sunday. “We pretty much stayed alive when nobody else thought we could. Now here we are.’’
The Red Sox were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East race on June 24. They have since gone 52-25 and will be in the playoffs.
The Red Sox lost 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, so couldn’t take care of things themselves. But about an hour after the game finished, the Houston Astros lost 4-2 to the Atlanta Braves, allowing the Red Sox to secure a wild-card spot.
Shortly after the Astros-Braves result went final, Red Sox players, coaches and staff members gathered near the Tropicana Field mound for a team photograph.
“I really don’t care how we got in, as long as we got in,’’ shortstop Trevor Story said.
Interim manager Chad Tracy was in place for much of the turnaround. Since being appointed on April 26 following the dismissal of Alex Cora, the Red Sox have gone 74-55.
“Look, we were not in a good spot,’’ Tracy said. “We were not playing good ball. But it shows you that if you stick to it, good things can happen. I couldn’t be more proud of this group.’’
First baseman Willson Contreras said he kept the faith, even when things trended downward, and the reward was sweet.
“It’s hard not to have some tears over this,’’ Contreras said. “It’s a great accomplishment, but I don’t want this team to stop here. I want to keep going. We have proven that you can get hot and overcome a lot of big odds.’’
___

item.title: [Boston Herald] ‘Battle-tested’ Red Sox eager to prove they’re ready for more in postseason
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox. The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are
item.content:encoded:
As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox.
The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are 9-9 this month, struggling offensively, without on several injured stars, and are their first postseason round will almost certainly be a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where they fell to their rivals 2-1.
In other words, there is much work to be done. The Red Sox know it, and they are eager to prove they did not come this far to only go this far.
“This has been a turbulent season,” Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow told reporters. “This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here.”
But neither the recent struggles nor the battles ahead should diminish the magnitude of the overall achievement of getting to this point.
The Red Sox lost American League Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet to a shoulder injury in mid-April, and he has yet to return.
They fired manager Alex Cora and several coaches in the middle of a late-April road series in Baltimore, and promoted Triple-A Worcester skipper Chad Tracy and several others from their minor league coaching ranks.
Injuries sidelined star outfielder Roman Anthony and veteran shortstop Trevor Story from early May until the very end of August.
The Red Sox owned their worst home record to start a season since 1932, and were 15 1/2 games out of first in the American League East in June.
On June 24, they fell to 14 games under .500. On Sunday, they became the fourth team in Major League Baseball history to go from as many as 14 games under .500 to the postseason in the same season.
“We needed time, and the time came for us,” veteran first baseman Willson Contreras told his teammates in the clubhouse. “I’m very proud of you all.”
“It’s 162 for a reason,” echoed third baseman Caleb Durbin.
“Obviously, getting where we want to go, but ultimately, what we had to overcome to get here makes it all the more sweet,” Tracy said. “We had a long way to go, and they never stopped, and they didn’t take no for an answer.”
This year looked lost, and the Red Sox managed to save it. They maintained an unshakeable belief in themselves, and it has already taken them to places most of the baseball world doubted it could go.
“Belief, belief, belief,” Contreras told reporters. “That was my main word, and that’s what I did from Day 1.”
The Red Sox are not a perfect team. But they certainly have the grit and gumption to go further than expected, as evidenced by the fact that they have already done so by reaching this point.
“We know how it felt when we left New York at the end of the year,” Story said. “You know how it made me feel. So that stayed with me.”
“They came together, and they found a way to get it done, and they had a long way to go to do it,” Tracy said. “They’re very battle-tested, and I’m super, super proud of them.”
“We don’t care where we play,” Tracy said. “You go back to July, and most people didn’t think we’d even be standing here. So it doesn’t matter where we play.”
“We’re in,” Tracy continued. “You got a ticket to the dance, and now you got to go take care of it there.”
“We’re in, baby,” Story said. “Let’s go.”
“Now, this is the moment,” right-fielder Wilyer Abreu said, “that we (were) waiting for.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox appear to be getting rotation in line for Wild Card Series - The Boston Globe

But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Y
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox's Curtis Mead Quietly Inching Closer to Playoff Return
item.dc:creator: Jackson Roberts; Unknown
item.description: Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact. In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress. According to a
item.content:encoded:
Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic.
